newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain regional debt offers competitive yields.
newsitem.headline: Spain regional debt offers competitive yields.

text.p: Investors hungry for high-yield can find in Spain more than one way to satisfy that demand -- along with Bonos, they can buy regional issues, analysts say.

With total debt having sky-rocketed to 4.261 trillion pesetas in June 1996 from 945 billion pesetas at the end of 1990, the 17 Spanish regional governments offer ample fare even for the heartiest appetites.
Spain's steps toward fiscal federalism have put growing demands on the regions' coffers, prompting a sharp rise in debt issuance across the country.
"Regional debt is not 100 percent like central government bonds, but it is really close and it offers higher yields," Manuel Navarro, dealer at Caja de Madrid, told Reuters.

Not all Spanish regional debt is tradeable. Up to June 1996 a mere 34 percent of the debt was in bonds, with the bulk made up of bank loans. But the most aggressive regions, such as Catalonia, are increasing the percentage of debt offered on the market.
Earlier this month, Catalonia inaugurated a new system of monthly public auctions, which should guarantee better liquidity and easier debt placement.

Valencia, which began a similar system a few years ago, is funding its debt at the cheapest rate among all regions. It usually offers a spread of some 15 basis points over 10-year bonos, while Catalonia has been paying 20 to 25 basis points over.
At an auction last week, Catalonia placed 10-year bonds at 15 points over Bonos of equivalent maturity, its cheapest 10-year funding ever.
Only Andalucia, Valencia and Catalonia have a regular system of public auction for bonds, organized similarly to central government bond auctions. They also offer short-term bills on a regular basis.
But to foreign investors, the secondary market can be cheaper than public auctions, because banks bid up the price of the paper in the highly competitive auctions.
"Many times these issues are cheaper on the secondary market," a dealer at Banco Central Hispano in Madrid said.
A dealer explained that financial institutions compete to offer good conditions to the regional governments in an effort to persuade the regions to bank with them.
Two of the regional governments, however, discourage foreign purchases of their debt.

Navarre and the Basque Country, which enjoy greater fiscal autonomy than other regions for historic reasons, do not place their debt outside Spain and do not reimburse foreign investors for witholding taxes.
Rating agencies publish ratings on only a few regions' debt.
Standard & Poor's has ratings on seven regions, ranging from Madrid with the lowest at AA minus to the Basque country at AA plus. The other five have been assigned an AA.
Moody's rates the Basque Country Aa2, while Valencia Castilla y Leon and Andalucia have all been rated Aa3. Catalonia and Madrid stand at A1, while Murcia is A2.
The regional issues are not legally backed by the Spanish government, but analysts said the central government might step in to help if necessary.
"We can't rule out that the state would intervene," said Jose Garcia, director in Standard and Poor's in Madrid.
In absolute terms, Catalonia has the highest level of debt, followed by Andalucia, Madrid and Valencia.
In relative terms, Murcia has the greater level of debt with a 163.5 of debt over revenue (at the end of 1994) followed by Madrid at 147.5 (end 1995).
